pages.x: In 1870 Europeans held only bits of Africa's coasts. Then quinine against malaria, steamboats and the rapid-firing machine gun made it possible to push inland, and rivalry among the powers made it urgent. Explorers like Henry Morton Stanley, who found the missing David Livingstone in 1871, showed the way.

In January 1879 a British army invaded the Zulu kingdom of Cetshwayo. At Isandlwana some 20,000 Zulu warriors, armed mostly with spears and shields, overran a British camp and killed more than 1,300 men, one of the worst defeats a colonial army ever suffered. Britain sent more troops, and by July the kingdom was broken.

In 1884 Bismarck invited the powers to Berlin to agree on rules for claiming Africa. Not one African was invited. The conference recognised the vast Congo as the private property of King Leopold II of Belgium, and agreed that a power could claim land if it really occupied it. The race to grab land speeded up.

Leopold ran the Congo as his own business. His agents forced villagers to gather wild rubber, holding wives hostage and cutting off hands when the quotas were not met. After a campaign by the reformer E. D. Morel and others, Belgium took the colony away from its king in 1908.

In 1896 Italy invaded Ethiopia. Emperor Menelik II, who had bought modern rifles and cannon, gathered an army of about 100,000 and, with Empress Taytu, met the Italians at Adwa. In one day the Italian army was destroyed. Italy had to recognise Ethiopia's independence, and Adwa became a symbol of pride for Black people everywhere.

Many Africans fought back. In West Africa Samori Ture built an empire with an army of riflemen, its guns copied and mended in his own workshops, and fought the French for 16 years, moving his whole state east when he had to. He was captured in 1898 and died in exile.

In 1900 the British governor of the Gold Coast demanded to sit on the Golden Stool, the sacred throne that held the soul of the Asante nation, which no one ever sat on. Yaa Asantewaa, queen mother of Ejisu, shamed the men by vowing that the women would fight if they would not, and led a rising that besieged the British fort in Kumasi.

By 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia were free. France held most of the northwest, Britain a chain of colonies from Egypt to the Cape, and Germany, Belgium, Portugal, Italy and Spain the rest. The new borders, ruled on maps in Europe, cut across hundreds of peoples and kingdoms.

Colonial rule brought railways, mines, schools and missions, but it was built on force and run for the rulers' profit, and it shaped Africa's borders, languages and trade to this day. Most African countries won back their freedom from the late 1950s to the 1970s, inside the borders that the scramble drew.
pts: A tenth of Africa was European in 1870, nine tenths by 1914
The rules were made in Berlin in 1884, with no Africans there
Ethiopia beat Italy at Adwa in 1896
